claim: The circadian clock governs rhythmic cellular functions by driving the expression of a substantial fraction of the genome.
source: The circadian clock governs rhythmic cellular functions by driving the expression of a substantial fraction of the genome and thereby significantly contributes to the adaptation to changing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about circadian clock function that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The circadian clock significantly contributes to the adaptation to changing environmental conditions.
source: The circadian clock governs rhythmic cellular functions by driving the expression of a substantial fraction of the genome and thereby significantly contributes to the adaptation to changing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript and represents established knowledge.

claim: Molecular timekeeping is robust even under severe limitation of carbon sources in Neurospora crassa.
source: Using the circadian model organism Neurospora crassa, we show that molecular timekeeping is robust even under severe limitation of carbon sources, however, stoichiometry, phosphorylation and subcellular distribution of the key clock components display drastic alterations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing clock function under starvation conditions.

claim: Stoichiometry, phosphorylation and subcellular distribution of the key clock components display drastic alterations under severe limitation of carbon sources.
source: Using the circadian model organism Neurospora crassa, we show that molecular timekeeping is robust even under severe limitation of carbon sources, however, stoichiometry, phosphorylation and subcellular distribution of the key clock components display drastic alterations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data and subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: Protein kinase A is involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock during glucose starvation.
source: Protein kinase A, protein phosphatase 2 A and glycogen synthase kinase are involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with the mcb mutant strain showing altered starvation response.

claim: Protein phosphatase 2A is involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock during glucose starvation.
source: Protein kinase A, protein phosphatase 2 A and glycogen synthase kinase are involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock.
evidence: This is supported by PP2A activity assays and experiments with the rgb-1 mutant.

claim: Glycogen synthase kinase is involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock during glucose starvation.
source: Protein kinase A, protein phosphatase 2 A and glycogen synthase kinase are involved in the molecular reorganization of the clock.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with the qa-gsk strain showing altered FRQ phosphorylation.

claim: The transcriptomic response of metabolism to starvation is highly dependent on the positive clock component WC-1.
source: RNA-seq analysis reveals that the transcriptomic response of metabolism to starvation is highly dependent on the positive clock component WC-1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing wt and Δwc-1 strains under starvation conditions.

claim: A functional clock facilitates recovery from starvation.
source: Moreover, our molecular and phenotypic data indicate that a functional clock facilitates recovery from starvation.
evidence: This is supported by growth recovery experiments comparing wt and clock mutants after glucose resupply.

claim: The molecular clock is a flexible network that allows the organism to maintain rhythmic physiology under long-term nutritional stress.
source: We suggest that the molecular clock is a flexible network that allows the organism to maintain rhythmic physiology and preserve fitness even under long-term nutritional stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing clock function under starvation.

claim: The molecular clock allows the organism to preserve fitness even under long-term nutritional stress.
source: We suggest that the molecular clock is a flexible network that allows the organism to maintain rhythmic physiology and preserve fitness even under long-term nutritional stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the recovery experiments showing better adaptation in wt compared to clock mutants.

claim: Circadian clocks rely on transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFL) in which positive elements activate the expression of oscillator proteins which in turn negatively feed back on their own transcription.
source: Circadian clocks rely on transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFL) in which positive elements of the machinery activate the expression of oscillator proteins which in turn negatively feed back on their own transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms.

claim: Circadian clocks are closely linked to metabolism.
source: Circadian clocks are closely linked to metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The clock rhythmically modulates many metabolic pathways.
source: On the one hand, the clock rhythmically modulates many metabolic pathways (Asher and Schibler, 2011; Huang et al., 2011; Bray and Young, 2011; Duez and Staels, 2009), and on the other hand, nutrients and metabolic cues influence clock function (e.g. Roenneberg and Rehman, 1996; Johnson, 1992; Stokkan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Nutrients and metabolic cues influence clock function.
source: On the one hand, the clock rhythmically modulates many metabolic pathways (Asher and Schibler, 2011; Huang et al., 2011; Bray and Young, 2011; Duez and Staels, 2009), and on the other hand, nutrients and metabolic cues influence clock function (e.g. Roenneberg and Rehman, 1996; Johnson, 1992; Stokkan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Conditions involving circadian rhythm dysfunction, such as shift work or jetlag, are associated with an increased risk of metabolic disorders including obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes in humans.
source: It is therefore not surprising that in human, conditions involving circadian rhythm dysfunction, such as shift work or jetlag, are associated with an increased risk of metabolic disorders including obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes (Baron and Reid, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The circadian oscillator was found to run with constant speed and maintain a constant period in Neurospora crassa.
source: Although the timing of nutrient availability as an important Zeitgeber determines the phase of the rhythm in many organisms, the circadian oscillator was found to run with constant speed and thus to maintain a constant period in the model organisms Neurospora crassa and Synechococcus elongatus (Sancar et al., 2012; Johnson and Egli, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The circadian oscillator was found to run with constant speed and maintain a constant period in Synechococcus elongatus.
source: Although the timing of nutrient availability as an important Zeitgeber determines the phase of the rhythm in many organisms, the circadian oscillator was found to run with constant speed and thus to maintain a constant period in the model organisms Neurospora crassa and Synechococcus elongatus (Sancar et al., 2012; Johnson and Egli, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glucose levels affect many signal transduction pathways in different organisms.
source: However, because glucose levels were shown to affect many signal transduction pathways as well as transcription and translation rates in different organisms (Ashe et al., 2000; Corral-Ramos et al., 2021; Jona et al., 2000; Sancar et al., 2012), glucose deficiency may challenge the TTFL-based circadian clock to operate at a constant period.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glucose levels affect transcription and translation rates in different organisms.
source: However, because glucose levels were shown to affect many signal transduction pathways as well as transcription and translation rates in different organisms (Ashe et al., 2000; Corral-Ramos et al., 2021; Jona et al., 2000; Sancar et al., 2012), glucose deficiency may challenge the TTFL-based circadian clock to operate at a constant period.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Neurospora the White-Collar-Complex (WCC) composed of the GATA-type transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2, and Frequency (FRQ) represent the core components of the circadian clock.
source: In Neurospora the White-Collar-Complex (WCC) composed of the GATA-type transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2, and Frequency (FRQ) represent the core components of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Neurospora circadian clock.

claim: The WCC supports expression of FRQ.
source: The WCC supports expression of FRQ which then interacts with an RNA helicase (FRH) and the casein kinase 1a (CK1a) (Cheng et al., 2005; Görl et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FRQ interacts with an RNA helicase (FRH) and the casein kinase 1a (CK1a).
source: The WCC supports expression of FRQ which then interacts with an RNA helicase (FRH) and the casein kinase 1a (CK1a) (Cheng et al., 2005; Görl et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The FRQ-FRH-CK1a complex acting as the negative factor of the clock facilitates phosphorylation and thus inhibition of the WCC.
source: The FRQ-FRH-CK1a complex acting as the negative factor of the clock facilitates phosphorylation and thus inhibition of the WCC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Neurospora circadian clock mechanism.

claim: During a circadian day FRQ is progressively phosphorylated, which reduces its inhibitory potential and leads to its degradation.
source: During a circadian day FRQ is progressively phosphorylated, which reduces its inhibitory potential and leads to its degradation (Querfurth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The negative feedback and the gradual maturation of FRQ together result in rhythmic changes of WCC activity and frq levels.
source: The negative feedback and the gradual maturation of FRQ together result in rhythmic changes of WCC activity and frq levels (Larrondo et al., 2015; Querfurth et al., 2011; Schafmeier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The negative feedback loop is connected to a positive loop, in which FRQ supports the accumulation of both WC-1 and WC-2.
source: The negative feedback loop is connected to a positive loop, in which FRQ supports the accumulation of both WC-1 and WC-2 (Cheng et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Neurospora circadian clock supports rhythmic expression of about 10% of the genome.
source: Similarly to other organisms, the Neurospora circadian clock supports rhythmic expression of about 10% of the genome (Hurley et al., 2014; Sancar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The WCC as the major photoreceptor of Neurospora is activated by light and thereby transduces light information to the clock.
source: The WCC as the major photoreceptor of Neurospora is activated by light and thereby transduces light information to the clock (Froehlich et al., 2002; He et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Short-term (0–16 hr) glucose deprivation triggers compensatory mechanisms at the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels that maintain expression levels of the core clock proteins in Neurospora.
source: In Neurospora, short-term (0–16 hr) glucose deprivation triggers compensatory mechanisms at the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels that maintain expression levels of the core clock proteins, thereby keeping period length constant (Adhvaryu et al., 2016; Emerson et al., 2015; Gyöngyösi et al., 2017; Olivares-Yañez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Short-term glucose deprivation keeps period length constant in Neurospora.
source: In Neurospora, short-term (0–16 hr) glucose deprivation triggers compensatory mechanisms at the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels that maintain expression levels of the core clock proteins, thereby keeping period length constant (Adhvaryu et al., 2016; Emerson et al., 2015; Gyöngyösi et al., 2017; Olivares-Yañez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The WCC has a striking impact on nutrient-dependent expression of a large set of genes, including enzymes and regulators of carbohydrate, amino acid, and fatty acid metabolism.
source: We analyzed the transcriptome response to long-term glucose starvation in wt and the clock-less mutant Δwc-1 and found that the WCC has a striking impact on nutrient-dependent expression of a large set of genes, including enzymes and regulators of carbohydrate, amino acid, and fatty acid metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing wt and Δwc-1 strains.

claim: The TTFL is able to function in a wide range of stoichiometric conditions of its key elements, dependent on glucose availability.
source: We show that molecular timekeeping is robust even under severe limitation of carbon sources. Moreover, our data provide evidence that the TTFL is able to function in a wide range of stoichiometric conditions of its key elements, dependent on glucose availability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing clock function despite altered protein levels.

claim: Neurospora recovers faster from starvation in the presence of a functioning clock.
source: Our results show that Neurospora recovers faster from starvation in the presence of a functioning clock, suggesting a significant impact of the circadian clock on organismal fitness.
evidence: This is supported by growth recovery experiments comparing wt and clock mutants.

claim: The circadian clock has a significant impact on organismal fitness.
source: Our results show that Neurospora recovers faster from starvation in the presence of a functioning clock, suggesting a significant impact of the circadian clock on organismal fitness.
evidence: This is inferred from the recovery experiments showing better adaptation in wt.

claim: Growth of Neurospora virtually stopped after transfer to starvation medium.
source: The growth of Neurospora virtually stopped after the medium change and the expression of the major clock components was characteristically changed compared to standard cultures (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WC-1 expression decreased gradually to about 15% of the initial levels after glucose deprivation.
source: Both WC-1 and WC-2 expression decreased gradually to about 15% and 20% of the initial levels, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data and densitometry analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WC-2 expression decreased gradually to about 20% of the initial levels after glucose deprivation.
source: Both WC-1 and WC-2 expression decreased gradually to about 15% and 20% of the initial levels, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data and densitometry analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amount of FRQ remained relatively constant after glucose deprivation.
source: The amount of FRQ remained relatively constant after glucose deprivation, but a mobility shift characteristic for hyperphosphorylation of the protein was observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A mobility shift characteristic for hyperphosphorylation of FRQ was observed after glucose deprivation.
source: The amount of FRQ remained relatively constant after glucose deprivation, but a mobility shift characteristic for hyperphosphorylation of the protein was observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B showing altered electrophoretic mobility.

claim: Hyperphosphorylated FRQ exerts a reduced negative feedback on WCC.
source: Because hyperphosphorylated FRQ exerts a reduced negative feedback on WCC (Schafmeier et al., 2006), we hypothesized that the starvation-induced phosphorylation of FRQ might lead to an increase in WCC activity and consequently to the acceleration of its decay (Kodadek et al., 2006; Punga et al., 2006; Schafmeier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased turnover of WC-1 may be, at least partially, responsible for the low WCC levels in the starved cells.
source: Our data suggest that increased turnover of WC-1 may be, at least partially, responsible for the low WCC levels in the starved cells.
evidence: This is inferred from cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNA levels of frq, wc-1 and wc-2 were similar under standard and glucose-starved conditions in constant light.
source: In LL WCC constantly promotes transcription of frq and wc-1. Although WCC levels were significantly different under standard and glucose-starved conditions, RNA levels of frq, wc-1 and wc-2 were similar (Figure 1C), suggesting a compensatory mechanism that either maintains the active pool of WCC under various nutritional conditions constant or stabilizes the RNA.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Changes in RNA stability do not contribute to the maintenance of frq levels during starvation.
source: In the next experiment we examined frq RNA levels after a light-dark transfer (LD), when transcription of frq is repressed, and therefore changes in frq levels reflect RNA degradation. frq RNA levels after LD transition were similar under both culture conditions, suggesting that changes in RNA stability do not contribute to the maintenance of frq levels during starvation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA decay experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FRQ protein showed a similar robust oscillation in both standard and starvation media in constant darkness.
source: We followed clock protein levels in constant darkness (DD), when the circadian clock displays a free running endogenous rhythm. FRQ protein showed a similar robust oscillation in both standard and starvation media, with no noticeable difference in period or phase (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot time course data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no noticeable difference in period or phase of FRQ oscillation between standard and starvation conditions.
source: FRQ protein showed a similar robust oscillation in both standard and starvation media, with no noticeable difference in period or phase (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot time course data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increased FRQ phosphorylation was observed under starvation conditions in constant light and at all time points in constant darkness.
source: When protein samples were analyzed on the same gel, increased FRQ phosphorylation was observed under starvation conditions in LL and at all time points in DD (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of WC proteins was greatly reduced in constant darkness upon glucose deprivation.
source: Similarly to the changes in LL, the expression of WC proteins was greatly reduced in DD upon glucose deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Neither phase nor amplitude of frq RNA oscillation was affected by starvation.
source: However, neither phase nor amplitude of frq RNA oscillation was affected by starvation (Figure 1G, left panel), indicating that WCC activity was similar under both conditions.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR time course data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: WCC activity was similar under both standard and starvation conditions.
source: However, neither phase nor amplitude of frq RNA oscillation was affected by starvation (Figure 1G, left panel), indicating that WCC activity was similar under both conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the maintained frq RNA levels despite reduced WCC protein levels.

claim: Starvation resulted in significant upregulation of ccg-2 expression.
source: To examine clock output function, we measured RNA levels of two clock-controlled genes, ccg-2 and fluffy (Bell-Pedersen et al., 1992). Similarly to previous findings, starvation resulted in significant upregulation of ccg-2 expression (Bell-Pedersen et al., 1992; Kaldenhoff and Russo, 1993; Sokolovsky et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G and citations to previous literature.

claim: Fluffy levels were elevated under starvation compared to standard conditions.
source: Interestingly, fluffy levels were also elevated under starvation compared to standard conditions.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A robust oscillation of ccg-2 and fluffy RNA was detected under both standard and starvation conditions, with peaks and troughs at the expected circadian time.
source: In addition, a robust oscillation of ccg-2 and fluffy RNA was detected under both conditions, with peaks and troughs at the expected circadian time (Figure 1G, right panel; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR time course data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The circadian clock functions robustly during glucose deprivation despite increased FRQ phosphorylation and decreased WCC levels.
source: Our results suggest that the circadian clock functions robustly during glucose deprivation despite increased FRQ phosphorylation and decreased WCC levels and drives rhythmic expression of output genes without changes in period length or phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing maintained clock function.

claim: The circadian clock drives rhythmic expression of output genes without changes in period length or phase during glucose deprivation.
source: Our results suggest that the circadian clock functions robustly during glucose deprivation despite increased FRQ phosphorylation and decreased WCC levels and drives rhythmic expression of output genes without changes in period length or phase.
evidence: This is supported by the oscillation data for frq, ccg-2, and fluffy RNA.

claim: The light-induced initial increase of RNA levels was lower in starved than non-starved cultures for frq, wc-1 and al-2.
source: To examine the activity of the WCC as the photoreceptor of Neurospora, we followed the expression of the light-inducible genes frq, wc-1 and al-2 after dark-light (DL) transfer under both nutrient conditions. The light-induced initial increase of RNA levels was lower in starved than non-starved cultures, whereas the steady state expression levels after light adaptation were similar under both conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The steady state expression levels of frq, wc-1 and al-2 after light adaptation were similar under both standard and starvation conditions.
source: The light-induced initial increase of RNA levels was lower in starved than non-starved cultures, whereas the steady state expression levels after light adaptation were similar under both conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The light-inducible pool or the photoreceptor function of WCC is reduced upon glucose deprivation.
source: The difference in the kinetics of light induction suggests that the light-inducible pool or the photoreceptor function of WCC is reduced upon glucose deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced light induction kinetics shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of FRQ was in the cytosol fraction, and its distribution did not change markedly upon glucose-deprivation.
source: In accordance with previous data (Cheng et al., 2005; Gyöngyösi et al., 2017; Schafmeier et al., 2006), the majority of FRQ was in the cytosol fraction, and its distribution did not change markedly upon glucose-deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous literature.

claim: WC proteins were virtually absent from the cytosol of starved cells.
source: In contrast, WC proteins were virtually absent from the cytosol of starved cells, whereas their nuclear concentrations were similar to those in the control cells.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nuclear concentrations of WC proteins were similar in starved and control cells.
source: In contrast, WC proteins were virtually absent from the cytosol of starved cells, whereas their nuclear concentrations were similar to those in the control cells.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Starvation did not alter frq expression in wt.
source: However, while starvation did not alter frq expression in wt, it decreased the amount of frq9 RNA (Figure 3A), resulting in similar RNA levels (reflecting similar frq promoter activity) in the two strains upon glucose withdrawal.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Starvation decreased the amount of frq9 RNA in the frq9 mutant.
source: However, while starvation did not alter frq expression in wt, it decreased the amount of frq9 RNA (Figure 3A), resulting in similar RNA levels (reflecting similar frq promoter activity) in the two strains upon glucose withdrawal.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FRQ-mediated processes contribute to the compensation of frq levels at different glucose availability.
source: The different behavior of frq promoter activity in frq9 and wt in response to glucose suggests that FRQ-mediated processes contribute to the compensation of frq levels at different glucose availability.
evidence: This is inferred from the different responses of frq and frq9 RNA to starvation.

claim: Amount of WC-1 did not change significantly in frq9 upon glucose deprivation.
source: Amount of WC-1 did not change significantly in frq9, whereas WC-2 levels were moderately reduced in response to glucose depletion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WC-2 levels were moderately reduced in frq9 in response to glucose depletion.
source: Amount of WC-1 did not change significantly in frq9, whereas WC-2 levels were moderately reduced in response to glucose depletion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FRQΔFCD1-2 displayed an electrophoretic mobility shift upon glucose withdrawal suggesting that starvation-induced phosphorylation of FRQ is not dependent on its interaction with CK1.
source: Upon glucose withdrawal FRQΔFCD1-2 also displayed an electrophoretic mobility shift suggesting that starvation-induced phosphorylation of FRQ is not dependent on its interaction with CK1.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ is not essential for the starvation-dependent hyperphosphorylation of FRQ.
source: Our data suggest that stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ is not essential for the starvation-dependent hyperphosphorylation of FRQ and the compensation of frq RNA, but it slightly affects glucose-dependent changes of the WC levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the frqΔFCD1-2 mutant data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ is not essential for the compensation of frq RNA during starvation.
source: Our data suggest that stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ is not essential for the starvation-dependent hyperphosphorylation of FRQ and the compensation of frq RNA, but it slightly affects glucose-dependent changes of the WC levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the frqΔFCD1-2 mutant data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ slightly affects glucose-dependent changes of the WC levels.
source: Our data suggest that stable recruitment of CK1a to FRQ is not essential for the starvation-dependent hyperphosphorylation of FRQ and the compensation of frq RNA, but it slightly affects glucose-dependent changes of the WC levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the frqΔFCD1-2 mutant data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both FRQ and WC-1 can be modified by PKA.
source: Both FRQ and WC-1 can be modified by PKA (Huang et al., 2007; Cha et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PKA activity decreases in both Neurospora and yeast when glucose is limited.
source: Moreover, PKA activity decreases in both Neurospora and yeast when glucose is limited (Conrad et al., 2014; Li and Borkovich, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FRQ protein level was high in mcb compared to wt.
source: In accordance with literature data, FRQ protein level was high in mcb compared to wt (Huang et al., 2007; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the mcb mutant glucose deprivation did not cause a reduction of WC-1 or WC-2 levels.
source: However, in the mutant glucose deprivation did not cause a reduction of WC-1 or WC-2 levels and frq RNA became elevated under starvation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the mcb mutant frq RNA became elevated under starvation.
source: However, in the mutant glucose deprivation did not cause a reduction of WC-1 or WC-2 levels and frq RNA became elevated under starvation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PKA plays a significant role in transducing starvation signals to the circadian clock.
source: This indicates that PKA plays a significant role in transducing starvation signals to the circadian clock.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered starvation response in the mcb mutant.

claim: GSK is an important factor of the starvation response in many organisms including yeast.
source: Glycogen synthase kinase (GSK) is an important factor of the starvation response in many organisms including yeast (Quan et al., 2015) and was shown to fine-tune the circadian period in Neurospora crassa (Tataroğlu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GSK was shown to fine-tune the circadian period in Neurospora crassa.
source: Glycogen synthase kinase (GSK) is an important factor of the starvation response in many organisms including yeast (Quan et al., 2015) and was shown to fine-tune the circadian period in Neurospora crassa (Tataroğlu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: WC-1 and FRQ levels were elevated in qa-gsk in the presence of 2% glucose.
source: According to previous findings (Tataroğlu et al., 2012), in the presence of 2% glucose WC-1 and FRQ levels were elevated in qa-gsk (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E and a citation to previous literature.

claim: WC levels were reduced in qa-gsk upon starvation, even to a higher extent than in wt.
source: While WC levels were reduced, even to a higher extent than in wt, FRQ did not become hyperphosphorylated and frq RNA levels moderately decreased upon starvation in the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FRQ did not become hyperphosphorylated in qa-gsk upon starvation.
source: While WC levels were reduced, even to a higher extent than in wt, FRQ did not become hyperphosphorylated and frq RNA levels moderately decreased upon starvation in the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: frq RNA levels moderately decreased upon starvation in qa-gsk.
source: While WC levels were reduced, even to a higher extent than in wt, FRQ did not become hyperphosphorylated and frq RNA levels moderately decreased upon starvation in the mutant.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GSK supports the hyperphosphorylation of FRQ during starvation.
source: These results suggest that GSK supports the hyperphosphorylation of FRQ during starvation, but this modulation of FRQ is not sufficient to impact WCC levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the qa-gsk mutant data showing lack of FRQ hyperphosphorylation.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of FRQ is not sufficient to impact WCC levels during starvation.
source: These results suggest that GSK supports the hyperphosphorylation of FRQ during starvation, but this modulation of FRQ is not sufficient to impact WCC levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the qa-gsk mutant data showing WCC reduction despite lack of FRQ hyperphosphorylation.

claim: PP2A is a major regulator of the clock affecting both FRQ and WCC.
source: PP2A is a major regulator of the clock affecting both FRQ and WCC (Colot et al., 2006; Gyöngyösi and Káldi, 2014; Querfurth et al., 2011; Schafmeier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PP2A activity is glucose-dependent in yeast.
source: Moreover, its activity is glucose-dependent in yeast (Hughes Hallett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Starvation decreases PP2A activity in Neurospora.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, starvation decreases PP2A activity also in Neurospora, to levels characteristic for the rgb-1 mutant, which lacks one of the regulatory subunits of the phosphatase complex.
evidence: This is supported by PP2A activity assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Starvation decreases PP2A activity to levels characteristic for the rgb-1 mutant.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, starvation decreases PP2A activity also in Neurospora, to levels characteristic for the rgb-1 mutant, which lacks one of the regulatory subunits of the phosphatase complex.
evidence: This is supported by PP2A activity assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Dephosphorylation of WC-2 in CHX-treated cells depends on PP2A.
source: We have previously shown that dephosphorylation of WC-2 in CHX-treated cells depends on PP2A (Gyöngyösi et al., 2013; Schafmeier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The delayed dephosphorylation of WC-2 observed in the starved cells can be a consequence of the decreased PP2A activity.
source: Hence, the delayed dephosphorylation of WC-2 observed in the starved cells compared to the control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) can be a consequence of the decreased PP2A activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the PP2A activity data and the WC-2 dephosphorylation kinetics.

claim: WC protein levels were not reduced in starved rgb-1.
source: Next, we examined the effect of glucose-starvation on the clock components in rgb-1. While frq RNA and FRQ protein levels were similar in wt and rgb-1, WC protein levels were not reduced in starved rgb-1 (Figure 3G), indicating that PP2A affects the glucose-dependent change in the stoichiometry of clock components.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: PP2A affects the glucose-dependent change in the stoichiometry of clock components.
source: Next, we examined the effect of glucose-starvation on the clock components in rgb-1. While frq RNA and FRQ protein levels were similar in wt and rgb-1, WC protein levels were not reduced in starved rgb-1 (Figure 3G), indicating that PP2A affects the glucose-dependent change in the stoichiometry of clock components.
evidence: This is inferred from the rgb-1 mutant data showing maintained WCC levels during starvation.

claim: Long-term glucose starvation affected more than 20% of coding genes at the level of RNA.
source: Long-term glucose starvation affected more than 20% of coding genes at the level of RNA.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The most upregulated genes in wt encode polysaccharide degrading enzymes, conidiation specific proteins and monosaccharide transporters.
source: The most upregulated genes in wt encode polysaccharide degrading enzymes, conidiation specific proteins and monosaccharide transporters, similarly to findings in Aspergillus niger (Nitsche et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1 and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Polysaccharide degrading enzymes (xylanases, endoglucanase) are considered scouting factors and their induction might play a foraging role increasing survival chances under starvation conditions.
source: Polysaccharide degrading enzymes (xylanases, endoglucanase) are considered scouting factors and their induction might play a foraging role increasing survival chances under starvation conditions (Benocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents speculation about the biological significance.

claim: Eleven out of the 15 genes that were the most upregulated in wt responded with a weaker or no increase to glucose-deprivation in ∆wc-1.
source: Eleven out of the 15 genes that were the most upregulated in wt responded with a weaker or no increase to glucose-deprivation in ∆wc-1, indicating a limited transcriptomic adaptation in the absence of the WCC (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: The absence of the WCC indicates a limited transcriptomic adaptation to starvation.
source: Eleven out of the 15 genes that were the most upregulated in wt responded with a weaker or no increase to glucose-deprivation in ∆wc-1, indicating a limited transcriptomic adaptation in the absence of the WCC (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data comparing wt and Δwc-1.

claim: A sum of 1377 RNAs representing 13% of the 9758 coding genes changed in a strain-specific manner in response to glucose starvation.
source: In a further analysis, we focused on physiologically more relevant differences and found that a sum of 1377 RNAs representing 13% of the 9758 coding genes changed in a strain-specific manner in response to glucose starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 90 out of the 1377 genes that changed in a strain-specific manner were reported to be direct targets of the WCC.
source: Based on literature data showing that the WCC affects the expression of several other transcription factors and controls basic cellular functions which might affect the expression of further genes, it was not surprising that only 90 out of the 1377 genes were reported to be direct targets of the WCC (Smith et al., 2010; Hurley et al., 2014; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published WCC target gene lists.

claim: 1348 genes displayed glucose-dependent difference showing that effect of wc-1 mutation on the transcriptome is highly nutrient-dependent.
source: Detailed comparison of the ∆wc-1/wt ratios of transcript levels revealed that 1348 genes displayed glucose-dependent difference showing that effect of wc-1 mutation on the transcriptome is highly nutrient-dependent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A substantial proportion of the genes responding differently to starvation in wt and ∆wc-1 is involved in crucial metabolic processes.
source: Using the Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment tool (Mi et al., 2013), we found that a substantial proportion of the genes responding differently to starvation in wt and ∆wc-1 is involved in crucial metabolic processes (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: In the wt the downregulation of biosynthetic processes of small molecules and amino acids dominated in response to starvation.
source: Further analysis showed that in the wt the downregulation of biosynthetic processes of small molecules and amino acids dominated, whereas Δwc-1 had a higher tendency to up-regulate amino acid catabolism and down-regulate fatty acid synthesis in response to long-term starvation (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Δwc-1 had a higher tendency to up-regulate amino acid catabolism in response to long-term starvation.
source: Further analysis showed that in the wt the downregulation of biosynthetic processes of small molecules and amino acids dominated, whereas Δwc-1 had a higher tendency to up-regulate amino acid catabolism and down-regulate fatty acid synthesis in response to long-term starvation (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Δwc-1 had a higher tendency to down-regulate fatty acid synthesis in response to long-term starvation.
source: Further analysis showed that in the wt the downregulation of biosynthetic processes of small molecules and amino acids dominated, whereas Δwc-1 had a higher tendency to up-regulate amino acid catabolism and down-regulate fatty acid synthesis in response to long-term starvation (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Pathways of fatty acid biosynthesis displayed the most uniform strain-dependent differences in response to starvation with a dominant downregulation in Δwc-1 compared to wt.
source: However, pathways of fatty acid biosynthesis displayed the most uniform strain-dependent differences in response to starvation with a dominant downregulation in Δwc-1 compared to wt (Figure 4—figure supplement 6, Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Tetrahydroxynaphthalene reductase-2 was strain-specifically upregulated in wt among constituents of fatty acid biosynthesis pathways.
source: Among constituents of these pathways only tetrahydroxynaphthalene reductase-2 was strain-specifically upregulated in wt (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: Tetrahydroxynaphthalene reductase catalyzes key steps of the synthesis of melanin, which is a crucial factor required for mechanical strength of cell wall.
source: Importantly, this enzyme catalyzes key steps of the synthesis of melanin, which is a crucial factor required for mechanical strength of cell wall and is therefore central in the adaptation to extreme changes in the environmental conditions (Nosanchuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Melanin is central in the adaptation to extreme changes in the environmental conditions.
source: Importantly, this enzyme catalyzes key steps of the synthesis of melanin, which is a crucial factor required for mechanical strength of cell wall and is therefore central in the adaptation to extreme changes in the environmental conditions (Nosanchuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All tested RNAs showed similar expression ratios in both RNA-seq and qRT-PCR analyses indicating the high reliability of the transcriptome profiling data.
source: To validate RNA-seq data, we performed qRT-PCR measurements for genes involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates or amino acids as well as for genes important for conidiation, the well-characterized nutrient-dependent process in fungi (Springer, 1993; Figure 4—figure supplement 7). All tested RNAs showed similar expression ratios in both analyses indicating the high reliability of our transcriptome profiling data (Figure 4—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The medium of starved wt cultures was cloudy before the addition of glucose, whereas the medium of clock-less cultures remained clear.
source: Interestingly, the medium of starved wt cultures was cloudy before the addition of glucose, whereas the medium of clock-less cultures remained clear (Figure 5B, Before: upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by visual observation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The cloudy material in starved wt cultures was constituted of small satellite colonies which might serve as a source for growth reinitiation.
source: As observed after filtration of the cultures (Figure 5B, Before: lower panel), the cloudy material was constituted of small satellite colonies which might serve as a source for growth reinitiation.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 5B and represents speculation about the biological function.

claim: The growth rate reflected by dry weight increase upon glucose resupply was higher in wt cultures than in frq10 and ∆wc-1.
source: Accordingly, the growth rate reflected by dry weight increase upon glucose resupply was higher in wt cultures than in frq10 and ∆wc-1, whereas non-starved control samples did not show strain-specific differences in the acceleration of growth after the transfer into fresh glucose-rich medium (Figure 5B, After, 5 C).
evidence: This is supported by dry weight measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Non-starved control samples did not show strain-specific differences in the acceleration of growth after the transfer into fresh glucose-rich medium.
source: Accordingly, the growth rate reflected by dry weight increase upon glucose resupply was higher in wt cultures than in frq10 and ∆wc-1, whereas non-starved control samples did not show strain-specific differences in the acceleration of growth after the transfer into fresh glucose-rich medium (Figure 5B, After, 5 C).
evidence: This is supported by dry weight measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Growth of both frq10 and ∆wc-1 was significantly slower than that of wt in constant darkness after glucose resupply.
source: To separate the clock and photoreceptor functions of the WCC in growth recovery, we repeated the experiment with cultures incubated in DD, that is when the WCC is not active as photoreceptor (Figure 5D). Growth of both frq10 and ∆wc-1 was significantly slower than that of wt, suggesting that presence of a functional clock supports regeneration upon glucose addition.
evidence: This is supported by dry weight measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Presence of a functional clock supports regeneration upon glucose addition.
source: Growth of both frq10 and ∆wc-1 was significantly slower than that of wt, suggesting that presence of a functional clock supports regeneration upon glucose addition.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth recovery experiments in DD.

claim: The growth rate of starved wt cultures approached that of the non-starved control during the second 6-hr period on race tubes.
source: Recovery from starvation was tested also on solid media by comparing growth rates following the transfer of mycelia from starved and control liquid cultures onto race tube medium which contained glucose (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Growth rates were determined for three consecutive periods. While the growth rate of starved wt cultures approached that of the non-starved control during the second 6-hr period, it remained at a low level in ∆wc-1, and slightly but significantly lagged behind the control rate also in frq10.
evidence: This is supported by race tube growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The growth rate of starved ∆wc-1 cultures remained at a low level on race tubes.
source: While the growth rate of starved wt cultures approached that of the non-starved control during the second 6-hr period, it remained at a low level in ∆wc-1, and slightly but significantly lagged behind the control rate also in frq10.
evidence: This is supported by race tube growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The growth rate of starved frq10 cultures slightly but significantly lagged behind the control rate on race tubes.
source: While the growth rate of starved wt cultures approached that of the non-starved control during the second 6-hr period, it remained at a low level in ∆wc-1, and slightly but significantly lagged behind the control rate also in frq10.
evidence: This is supported by race tube growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Neurospora, a dual-affinity transport system mechanism enables the proper adaptation of glucose uptake to external glucose levels.
source: In Neurospora, a dual-affinity transport system mechanism enables the proper adaptation of glucose uptake to external glucose levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Neurospora glucose transport.

claim: When glucose levels are elevated, increased expression of the low-affinity and high-capacity transporter, glt-1 ensures efficient utilization of the carbon source.
source: When glucose levels are elevated, increased expression of the low-affinity and high-capacity transporter, glt-1 ensures efficient utilization of the carbon source (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The transcriptomic analysis revealed higher glt-1 levels in non-starved than starved wt cells.
source: Accordingly, the transcriptomic analysis revealed higher glt-1 levels in non-starved than starved wt cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In ∆wc-1, glt-1 was upregulated under starvation conditions.
source: In ∆wc-1, however, glt-1 was upregulated under starvation conditions, indicating that the WCC is crucial in the adaptation of glucose transport to nutrient levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The WCC is crucial in the adaptation of glucose transport to nutrient levels.
source: In ∆wc-1, however, glt-1 was upregulated under starvation conditions, indicating that the WCC is crucial in the adaptation of glucose transport to nutrient levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the aberrant glt-1 expression in Δwc-1.

claim: In wt, glt-1 RNA levels gradually increased upon supplementation of the starvation medium with 2% glucose.
source: Next, we examined glt-1 expression during recovery. In wt, glt-1 RNA levels gradually increased upon supplementation of the starvation medium with 2% glucose.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression of glt-1 was relatively high in ∆wc-1 and frq10 under starvation.
source: In contrast, expression of glt-1 was relatively high in ∆wc-1 and frq10 under starvation, whereas it decreased or showed no change upon glucose addition, indicating that adaptation of the transporter level to glucose availability is disturbed in the clock mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: glt-1 expression decreased or showed no change upon glucose addition in ∆wc-1 and frq10.
source: In contrast, expression of glt-1 was relatively high in ∆wc-1 and frq10 under starvation, whereas it decreased or showed no change upon glucose addition, indicating that adaptation of the transporter level to glucose availability is disturbed in the clock mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Adaptation of the transporter level to glucose availability is disturbed in the clock mutants.
source: In contrast, expression of glt-1 was relatively high in ∆wc-1 and frq10 under starvation, whereas it decreased or showed no change upon glucose addition, indicating that adaptation of the transporter level to glucose availability is disturbed in the clock mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the aberrant glt-1 expression patterns in clock mutants.

claim: The marked differences between the recovery behavior of the different strains suggest that adaptation to changing nutrient availability is more efficient when a circadian clock operates in the cell.
source: In summary, the marked differences between the recovery behavior of the different strains suggest that adaptation to changing nutrient availability is more efficient when a circadian clock operates in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the recovery experiments.

claim: Deprivation of carbon sources reduces the transcription/translation rate.
source: In nature, the reproductive capacity of living things exceeds the availability of resources, and organisms face nutrient shortages from time to time. Optimal metabolic responses to nutrient deficiencies can therefore provide a significant advantage in selection. Deprivation of carbon sources reduces the transcription/translation rate, which is also a challenge for the TTFL-based molecular clock.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular responses to nutrient deprivation.

claim: Short glucose deprivation does not affect expression of the core clock proteins in Neurospora.
source: Short glucose deprivation does not affect expression of the core clock proteins in Neurospora and this maintenance of the protein levels was considered essential for nutrient-compensation (Emerson et al., 2015; Gyöngyösi et al., 2017; Sancar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maintenance of the protein levels was considered essential for nutrient-compensation.
source: Short glucose deprivation does not affect expression of the core clock proteins in Neurospora and this maintenance of the protein levels was considered essential for nutrient-compensation (Emerson et al., 2015; Gyöngyösi et al., 2017; Sancar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The circadian TTFL functions with substantially altered levels and stoichiometry of its key elements during long-term glucose starvation.
source: Our experiments show that the circadian TTFL functions with substantially altered levels and stoichiometry of its key elements during long-term glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Cytosolic but not nuclear WC protein levels are primarily reduced under low glucose conditions.
source: Importantly, cytosolic but not nuclear WC protein levels are primarily reduced under low glucose conditions.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cytosolic WCC might serve as a reserve pool of the positive factor that can be rapidly activated by Zeitgebers to synchronize the clock with the changing environment.
source: Cytosolic WCC might serve as a reserve pool of the positive factor that can be rapidly activated by Zeitgebers (e.g. light) to synchronize the clock with the changing environment (Malzahn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The maintained nuclear levels of the WCC might contribute to the preserved function of the circadian clock under starvation.
source: However, the maintained nuclear levels of the WCC might contribute to the preserved function of the circadian clock under starvation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the subcellular fractionation data.

claim: Presence of a functional circadian clock significantly affects the adaptation of Neurospora crassa to long-term glucose deprivation.
source: Our results indicate that presence of a functional circadian clock significantly affects the adaptation of Neurospora crassa to long-term glucose deprivation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the recovery experiments and transcriptomic data.

claim: Starved wt cultures better adapt the expression of the high-capacity glucose transporter to glucose levels than clock-less cultures.
source: Starved wt cultures better adapt the expression of the high-capacity glucose transporter to glucose levels and grow faster in both LD and DD upon resupply of glucose than clock-less cultures.
evidence: This is supported by glt-1 expression and growth recovery data.

claim: More than 1300 coding genes displayed different response to glucose starvation in wt and ∆wc-1.
source: Accordingly, we found that more than 1300 coding genes displayed different response to glucose starvation in wt and ∆wc-1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The lack of WCC resulted in a characteristic shift from the control of central carbon metabolism and the downregulation of amino acid synthesis to the upregulation of amino acid catabolism and the downregulation of fatty acid synthesis.
source: The lack of WCC resulted in a characteristic shift from the control of central carbon metabolism and the downregulation of amino acid synthesis to the upregulation of amino acid catabolism and the downregulation of fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by GO and KEGG pathway analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The WCC is an important determinant of the adaptive reorganization of the transcriptome in response to critical changes in glucose supply.
source: This means that the WCC is an important determinant of the adaptive reorganization of the transcriptome in response to critical changes in glucose supply.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Glucose availability was shown to act as an effective Zeitgeber at different levels of the phylogenetic hierarchy.
source: Glucose availability was shown to act as an effective Zeitgeber at different levels of the phylogenetic hierarchy, with detailed investigations in Arabidopsis thaliana, Drosophila melanogaster and mammalian systems (Frank et al., 2018; Kaasik et al., 2013; Hirota et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila starvation resistance is reduced in the clock mutants per01 and tim01.
source: In Drosophila starvation resistance is reduced in the clock mutants per01 and tim01(Kaasik et al., 2013; Schäbler et al., 2020), also indicating that endogenous time measuring helps to adapt to critical metabolic conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endogenous time measuring helps to adapt to critical metabolic conditions.
source: In Drosophila starvation resistance is reduced in the clock mutants per01 and tim01(Kaasik et al., 2013; Schäbler et al., 2020), also indicating that endogenous time measuring helps to adapt to critical metabolic conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the Drosophila studies cited.

claim: In mouse fibroblasts normal amplitude cycling of PER2 was detected for several days upon glucose depletion.
source: In mouse fibroblasts normal amplitude cycling of PER2 was detected for several days upon glucose depletion, indicating that, similarly to our findings in Neurospora, the clock function is preserved during critical metabolic conditions in mammalian cells as well (Putker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The clock function is preserved during critical metabolic conditions in mammalian cells.
source: In mouse fibroblasts normal amplitude cycling of PER2 was detected for several days upon glucose depletion, indicating that, similarly to our findings in Neurospora, the clock function is preserved during critical metabolic conditions in mammalian cells as well (Putker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No data are available about the effect of starvation on the molecular network of the clock in any other organisms than Neurospora.
source: However, still no data are available about the effect of starvation on the molecular network of the clock in any other organisms than Neurospora.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The WCC has a major impact on the mechanisms balancing the cellular energy state in Neurospora.
source: In conclusion, our results suggest that the WCC has a major impact on the mechanisms balancing the cellular energy state in Neurospora and highlight the importance of the circadian clock in cell survival under nutritional stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The circadian clock is important for cell survival under nutritional stress.
source: In conclusion, our results suggest that the WCC has a major impact on the mechanisms balancing the cellular energy state in Neurospora and highlight the importance of the circadian clock in cell survival under nutritional stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of FRQ observed in starvation weakens the inhibitory feedback on the WCC which might contribute to the compensation for the reduced transcription/translation rate during nutrient shortage.
source: A possible explanation is that hyperphosphorylation of FRQ observed in starvation weakens the inhibitory feedback on the WCC which might contribute to the compensation for the reduced transcription/translation rate during nutrient shortage but also leads to faster degradation of the WCC (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of FRQ leads to faster degradation of the WCC.
source: A possible explanation is that hyperphosphorylation of FRQ observed in starvation weakens the inhibitory feedback on the WCC which might contribute to the compensation for the reduced transcription/translation rate during nutrient shortage but also leads to faster degradation of the WCC (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The starvation-dependent reduced stability of WC-1 in wt supports the concept that hyperphosphorylation of FRQ leads to faster degradation of the WCC.
source: The starvation-dependent reduced stability of WC-1 in wt supports this concept.
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absence of FRQ-dependent feedback on the WCC might explain why WCC levels are only moderately affected by starvation in frq9.
source: The absence of FRQ-dependent feedback on the WCC might explain why WCC levels are only moderately affected by starvation in frq9.
evidence: This is speculation based on the frq9 mutant data.

claim: Starvation can not decrease WCC levels efficiently below a minimum level in frq9.
source: On the other hand, in frq9 WCC levels are low even under standard glucose conditions, raising the possibility that starvation can not decrease it efficiently, that is, below a minimum level.
evidence: This is speculation based on the frq9 mutant data.

claim: Elevation of the glucose level seems to increase the amount of the WCC in a FRQ-dependent manner.
source: However, when analysed from another perspective, elevation of the glucose level seems to increase the amount of the WCC in a FRQ-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing wt and frq9 responses to glucose.

claim: The starvation-dependent decrease in frq9 RNA abundance suggests that in the absence of the feedback mechanism the starvation-induced reduction of the global transcription rate cannot be compensated by an increase of the WCC activity.
source: The starvation-dependent decrease in frq9 RNA abundance also suggests that in the absence of the feedback mechanism the starvation-induced reduction of the global transcription rate cannot be compensated by an increase of the WCC activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the frq9 mutant data.

claim: The earlier described difference in the frq promoter activity between wt and frq9 is absent under starvation conditions.
source: Our findings reveal that the earlier described difference in the frq promoter activity between wt and frq9 (Schafmeier et al., 2005) is absent under starvation conditions, that is, the phenotype of the mutant is nutrient-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by the frq9 RNA data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The phenotype of the frq9 mutant is nutrient-dependent.
source: Our findings reveal that the earlier described difference in the frq promoter activity between wt and frq9 (Schafmeier et al., 2005) is absent under starvation conditions, that is, the phenotype of the mutant is nutrient-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the frq9 RNA data under different glucose conditions.

claim: The glucose-dependent modulation of the clock is probably not restricted to changes in the FRQ-dependent recruitment of CK1a to the WCC.
source: The glucose-dependent modulation of the clock is probably not restricted to changes in the FRQ-dependent recruitment of CK1a to the WCC, as the impaired interaction between FRQ and CK1a in the frqΔFCD1-2 strain only partially affected WCC level alterations and did not change frq RNA level.
evidence: This is inferred from the frqΔFCD1-2 mutant data.

claim: CK-1 independent mechanisms might be responsible for the starvation-induced phosphorylation of FRQ.
source: In addition, the starvation-induced phosphorylation of FRQ was preserved in the mutant suggesting that CK-1 independent mechanisms might be responsible for it.
evidence: This is speculation based on the frqΔFCD1-2 mutant data.

claim: Starvation triggers characteristic changes in the activity of signaling routes that affect basic components of the circadian clock.
source: Starvation triggers characteristic changes in the activity of signaling routes that affect basic components of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutant analysis data.

claim: PP2A was described as glucose sensitive regulator in fungal as well as in mammalian cells.
source: PP2A was described as glucose sensitive regulator in fungal as well as in mammalian cells (Hughes Hallett et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018) and we showed that glucose starvation decreases PP2A activity in Neurospora.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PP2A is known to act on both the negative and the positive element of the Neurospora clock.
source: PP2A is known to act on both the negative and the positive element of the Neurospora clock (Schafmeier et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reduced PP2A activity during nutrient limitation may contribute to the hyperphosphorylation of FRQ which lessens the negative feedback on the WCC activity.
source: Reduced PP2A activity during nutrient limitation may contribute to the hyperphosphorylation of FRQ which lessens the negative feedback on the WCC activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the PP2A activity data and knowledge of PP2A function.

claim: The activator effect of reduced PP2A activity might be antagonized by a weaker dephosphorylation of the WC proteins.
source: However, this activator effect might be antagonized by a weaker dephosphorylation of the WC proteins.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge of PP2A function on WC proteins.

claim: Starvation-dependent expression change of the WCC is dependent on PP2A.
source: In the rgb-1 strain in which one of the regulatory subunits of PP2A is disrupted and the enzyme activity is rather low, WC levels did not respond to glucose-deprivation, suggesting that starvation-dependent expression change of the WCC is dependent on PP2A.
evidence: This is inferred from the rgb-1 mutant data.

claim: Starvation triggers activation of GSK in many organisms.
source: Starvation triggers activation of GSK in many organisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the literature.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of FRQ upon glucose depletion is dependent on GSK.
source: Our data indicate that hyperphosphorylation of FRQ upon glucose depletion is dependent on GSK.
evidence: This is supported by the qa-gsk mutant data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Whether FRQ is a direct substrate of GSK, is still to be elucidated.
source: Whether FRQ is a direct substrate of GSK, is still to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Reduced PKA activity in starvation is considered as a central organizer of the cellular adaptation to nutrient restriction.
source: Reduced PKA activity in starvation is considered as a central organizer of the cellular adaptation to nutrient restriction (Huang et al., 2007; Li and Borkovich, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PKA is a priming kinase for subsequent phosphorylation of the WCC by CK1a and/or CK2, contributing to inactivation of the transcription factor.
source: PKA is a priming kinase for subsequent phosphorylation of the WCC by CK1a and/or CK2, contributing to inactivation of the transcription factor (Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The weakened inhibition by PKA might ensure that transcriptional activity of the WCC is preserved during starvation in both DD and LL.
source: Thus, in addition to the reduced feedback by FRQ, the weakened inhibition by PKA might also ensure that transcriptional activity of the WCC is preserved during starvation in both DD and LL.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge of PKA function and the experimental findings.

claim: PKA increases FRQ stability.
source: However, since PKA increases FRQ stability (Huang et al., 2007), affects translation under stress conditions (Barraza et al., 2017; Leipheimer et al., 2019) and activates PP2A in yeast (Castermans et al., 2012), it may also influence the clock via these functions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PKA affects translation under stress conditions.
source: However, since PKA increases FRQ stability (Huang et al., 2007), affects translation under stress conditions (Barraza et al., 2017; Leipheimer et al., 2019) and activates PP2A in yeast (Castermans et al., 2012), it may also influence the clock via these functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PKA activates PP2A in yeast.
source: However, since PKA increases FRQ stability (Huang et al., 2007), affects translation under stress conditions (Barraza et al., 2017; Leipheimer et al., 2019) and activates PP2A in yeast (Castermans et al., 2012), it may also influence the clock via these functions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The enhanced PKA activity in the mcb strain interfered with all observed starvation-induced changes within the molecular oscillator.
source: Indeed, the enhanced PKA activity in the mcb strain interfered with all observed starvation-induced changes within the molecular oscillator.
evidence: This is supported by the mcb mutant data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PKA acts as a main coordinator of the adaptation of the circadian clock to different nutrient conditions.
source: In conclusion, our observations along with literature data suggest a model in which PKA acts as a main coordinator of the adaptation of the circadian clock to different nutrient conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and literature, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The nutrient-dependent activity of multiple signaling pathways might ensure that the transcriptional activity of the WCC and thus expression and oscillation of frq remain nutrient-compensated.
source: Overall, the nutrient-dependent activity of multiple signaling pathways might ensure that the transcriptional activity of the WCC and thus expression and oscillation of frq remain nutrient-compensated.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings with multiple mutants.
